questions.q: Why does Mrs Lithebe reproach Gertrude at the start of the chapter?
choices: For spending too much money
For speaking and laughing 'idly and carelessly' with people who are not decent — in a house where the umfundisi has 'suffered enough'
For leaving the house without permission
For quarrelling with the girl
questions.explain: Gertrude answers that she will be glad to leave Johannesburg: 'I do not know what to do in this place.'

questions.q: What does the stout woman bring to the house?
choices: Food for the party
A newspaper with a fresh headline: 'ANOTHER MURDER TRAGEDY IN CITY. EUROPEAN HOUSEHOLDER SHOT DEAD BY NATIVE HOUSEBREAKER'
A letter from Absalom
News that the trial is over
questions.explain: It is 'a hard thing that this should happen at this moment', just as the case is to finish.

questions.q: What do the women do about the newspaper?
choices: Show it to Kumalo at once
Hide it, and arrange for everyone to eat at Mrs Lithebe's so Kumalo will not see it at the Mission House
Burn it
Send it back with the woman
questions.explain: Msimangu notes Kumalo does not read the paper on days they go to the case.

questions.q: Why does timing of such a headline matter so much just now?
choices: It could delay the trial
A fresh 'native housebreaker' murder in the news could harden feeling against Absalom just as the judge is deciding
It might frighten Mrs Lithebe out of her house
It has nothing to do with the case
questions.explain: The women fear it will make the judgement heavier.

questions.q: What 'feeling' does Gertrude confide to Mrs Lithebe?
choices: That she wants to go back to her old life
That perhaps she should become a nun and renounce the world, after hearing a black sister speak
That she wants to stay in Johannesburg
That she is angry with Kumalo
questions.explain: Mrs Lithebe claps her hands — 'not because you should do it, but because you should think of it.'

questions.q: What is the difficulty with Gertrude's idea of becoming a nun?
choices: She is not baptised
There is her small boy to care for
The church would not allow a black nun
She has no money for it
questions.explain: Gertrude wonders whether Kumalo's wife, or the girl, would care for him better.

questions.q: How does the girl respond when asked whether she would care for the boy?
choices: Reluctantly
Eagerly — 'Indeed I should care for him... As though he were my own'
She refuses
She says she is too young
questions.explain: The girl also promises she does not 'talk carelessly any more.'

questions.q: What do Mrs Lithebe and Gertrude agree about the plan for now?
choices: To tell Kumalo at once
To keep it 'unspoken except between us', pray about it, and speak again after a time
To ask the Bishop
To abandon it
questions.explain: If it happens, Mrs Lithebe says, 'it will comfort the old man.'

questions.q: What kind of 'laughter' does Mrs Lithebe object to throughout these scenes?
choices: Laughter at funerals
'Careless' laughter — idle, thoughtless talk that does not befit a house of suffering
Loud laughter that wakes the child
Laughter at her cooking
questions.explain: She says there is 'one kind of laughter, and there is another.'

questions.q: What does this quiet domestic chapter set against the courtroom chapters around it?
choices: Comic relief only
The women's care, faith and small acts of protection for Kumalo — mending and holding the household together
A subplot about money
Nothing; it is unrelated
questions.explain: Mrs Lithebe's refrain: 'Why else do we live?'
